Shug’s Bagels Brings a Taste of NYC to ATX

Fresh bagels, long lines, and a touch of chaos included
by Darcie Duttweiler November 12, 2026November 12, 2026

Walking into Shug’s Bagels gave me a weird sense-memory. It’s familiar, yet not. It smells of boiling bagels, and a line snakes out of the green-tiled lobby. But I can close my eyes and still see Austin Java. 

When I first moved from the ’burbs to Austin proper, I lived in an apartment off Enfield. Clarksville was somehow affordable to two twentysomethings back then. Austin Java was one of the closest places within walking distance, a novelty for someone who grew up where driving everywhere was the norm. I spent countless nights there, and the layout is burned into my brain. After two long years of seeing the Shug’s sign up without the place opening, I was curious how it’d turn out.

Dallas-launched Shug’s built a following for its East Coast deli approach before expanding to New Orleans and eventually Austin. Permitting and utility delays pushed back the opening, and the restaurant finally welcomed customers in August.

Full transparency: I’m not a bagel connoisseur, although I lived in the Big Apple for a semester in college and ate my fair share. Shug’s makes its bagels the old-school way, boiling them before baking for a dense, chewy interior and glossy crust. I prefer a chew and a light toast. I love lox, and I legit adore cream cheese. But I also abhor lines. So, my first visit gave me plenty to consider.

I arrived around 9:15am on a Monday morning to find a short line and a bustling dining room. Behind the counter, bagels bubbled away in boiling water. People crowded around the lobby waiting for their orders, and the line grew steadily as the morning wore on.

The space is a convincing old-school deli, with checkerboard floors, dark pressed-tin ceilings, green leather booths, and amber pendant lights. A sprawling gallery wall incorporates vintage signs and an oversized orange Austin Java marquee, another nod to the past. There are also framed retro Playboy covers featuring models wearing bagels as a bra. Shug’s takes its bagels seriously without taking itself too seriously.

The front patio is open and sociable, but the back patio is the real destination. Tucked behind the building, it’s full of hanging greenery and feels worlds away from the lobby commotion. The downstairs dining room is similarly tranquil, and both are better bets if the crowd feels chaotic. Parking is more of a challenge. The lot is tiny and oddly shaped, and the lobby can get crowded as the line grows.

Starting with the Breakfast Shug: The enormous sandwich is served untoasted, and I wasn’t entirely sure how to tackle it. Egg, cheese, bacon, and a hash brown are tucked inside, and that potato patty stays remarkably crisp beneath the mountain of ingredients – even when reheated for lunch later. The bright-yellow egg everything bagel had a great bite, and the fillings were well proportioned.

Going for a classic order, the whole-wheat everything bagel with lox spread was another story. The dill-heavy mixture was piled on so thickly that my husband scraped some off. “It’s so much schmear I don’t get to appreciate the bagel,” he said. Fair point. It was delicious, but the sheer quantity overwhelmed the bread.

Here’s where ordering at Shug’s gets weird. The default spread portion is 4 ounces, but a smaller, cheaper 2-ounce serving is available. I didn’t realize I could choose a different amount until after the fact. Menu prices seem reasonable until the à la carte add-ons show up on the receipt. Want the pizza bagel open-faced? That’s another dollar, even though it comes that way. None of these charges are totally outrageous, but the extra costs aren’t obvious ahead of time, and it feels a little nickel-and-dime-y when you see it printed out. Just know your options before ordering, especially if a heavy-handed schmear isn’t your ideal.

That being said, a black-and-white cookie was a decent finish to breakfast, even though the white side had thicker icing and a sturdier cookie while the chocolate side was softer and a little floppier.

On my return visit, a Saturday afternoon before a big UT game, the patio was packed with burnt orange, and the line was exactly what I’d hoped to avoid. Since every order comes in a to-go bag anyway, I’d ordered ahead online and took my lunch downstairs, away from the hubbub.

I started with the turkey sandwich on an onion bagel. The deli turkey was thickly sliced and piled high with plenty of lettuce and tomato. The sandwich was huge, and the lightly toasted bagel still had plenty of chew with a little crunch around the edges. I liked this one better than the lox spread bagel because I could actually taste the bread. My husband also clocked the double slices of cheese, which reminded him of sandwiches his mum made.

The chopped cheese on a roll was gloriously gooey and sloppy – basically a gloopy cheeseburger, which isn’t a criticism. There were so many red onions that their sharpness lingered long after, but the beef, cheese, and sauce made for an extremely satisfying lunch. I wisely skipped a bagel, and the roll held up to the filling without making it difficult to eat.

Shug’s also has an entire section devoted to chicken cutlet sandwiches, with combos including melted Muenster and Russian dressing; bacon and barbecue sauce; or Buffalo sauce, coleslaw, and pickles. I didn’t get to try any, but the lineup feels tailor-made for a hungover Sunday.

The open-faced pizza bagel was tasty, if greasy. Cupping pepperoni held little pools of oil, and it was blanketed in mozzarella. I could’ve used a little more marinara, but I’d happily eat it again. I took home leftovers, reheated them in the toaster oven, and served them to friends during the game. They were demolished in seconds.

I also brought home a French toast bagel, a blueberry bagel, and vanilla walnut cream cheese for breakfast the next morning. Toasted at home, both bagels were pillowy inside with a crisp exterior. Applying my own – substantially less aggressive – amount of spread made for a better balance.

Between the chewy bagels, hearty sandwiches, and surprisingly Zen-like back patio, Shug’s has plenty going for it. The crowd and the weird add-on pricing are less than ideal, but neither is a dealbreaker. Next time, I’ll just order less schmear. Even I have my limits.

Shug’s Bagels

1206 Parkway 
shugsbagels.com
